trace: The Global Value and Momentum strategy mixes two well-documented premia — value (Book-to-Price, P/E) and momentum (6- and 12-month returns) — drawn from the MSCI World universe. My first task is to identify what factor model actually explains its returns. The Fama-French 5-factor plus momentum model captures 78% of variance over 2010-2023, with the two intended loadings being the dominant drivers: HML at 0.48 contributing roughly 3.5% annualized and UMD at 0.55 contributing 4.1%. That leaves a statistically significant annualized alpha around 2.1% (t-stat 2.58), suggesting genuine stock-selection skill on top of the factor tilts. The tension in evaluating this strategy is that combining value and momentum is theoretically sound — the two factors are negatively correlated, so blending them should dampen crash risk — yet the implementation mechanics introduce exposures the manager never explicitly targeted. I notice a persistent negative QMJ loading of -0.21, meaning the portfolio systematically holds lower-quality firms. This makes sense because cheap stocks on Book-to-Price and P/E often carry distressed balance sheets, and the momentum screen does not filter on profitability. The SMB loading of 0.19 indicates a small-cap tilt that quietly adds return volatility. The time dimension matters here: Value exposure decayed from 0.65 in 2011 to 0.30 in 2021, likely because value spreads compressed during the decade-long growth rally and the composite score started tilting toward momentum names. Simultaneously the Investment factor (CMA) loading turned more negative, signaling a drift toward aggressively investing firms. The unintended quality drag is the most actionable finding — incorporating a simple profitability screen into the composite score is projected to lift the Sharpe by 0.22 and shrink maximum drawdown by 15%. The quarterly rebalancing is a reasonable trade-off on costs but leaves the strategy exposed to sharp momentum reversals that move faster than a quarter.

The QARP US Equity strategy blends quality (60% weight using ROE, debt-to-equity, earnings stability) and value (40% weight using P/E, P/B, FCF Yield) drawn from the Russell 1000. Over 12 years it has achieved a Sharpe of 1.15, which is genuinely strong for a long-only equity product. Factor attribution shows 78% of returns are explained by documented factors, with Quality driving 45% of total return, Value 22%, and Market Beta 11%. The remaining 22% is strategy-specific alpha significant at the 99% confidence level (p-value 0.009), suggesting the composite score has genuine stock-selection content beyond mechanical factor tilts. The central tension is that the value component — particularly the P/B screen — inadvertently produces a persistent negative momentum loading of -0.31 because stocks that look cheap on price-to-book have typically underperformed recently, placing them on the wrong side of UMD. This negative momentum bet has detracted an estimated 8% from cumulative returns over the full period and creates sharp underperformance precisely during the momentum-driven rallies that are hardest to explain to clients. I find it notable that this exposure has deepened over the last four years, which aligns with the massive momentum dispersion of 2020-2021 when growth names dominated. The fix the analysis points to — replacing P/B with EV/EBITDA — would reduce the negative momentum beta from -0.31 to -0.22 because EV/EBITDA is less mechanically opposed to recent price performance. A portfolio-level momentum-neutralization overlay is the more surgical option projected to add 0.20 to the Sharpe. Semi-annual rebalancing instead of quarterly would preserve 95% of alpha while cutting turnover almost in half, meaningfully reducing the estimated 40 basis points of annual transaction cost drag.

The 9-month momentum strategy selecting the top 30 US equities by price performance and rebalancing quarterly produced a Sharpe of 1.15 over 15 years but collapsed to 0.40 over the most recent three years. My goal is to separate structural decay from cyclical factor headwinds. Over the full period, 68% of returns are explained by factors, with UMD accounting for 55%, SMB 8%, and a negative HML tilt at -5% consistent with momentum portfolios concentrating in growth names. The strategy generated annualized alpha of 2.9% after Fama-French 5-factor adjustment (t-stat 2.95, p-value 0.003), and the deflated Sharpe of 0.88 indicates genuine skill, though a 24% CSCV overfitting probability warrants caution. The recent deterioration breaks down as 70% attributable to poor momentum factor performance itself — the broad UMD factor suffered losses in the choppy, mean-reverting tape of 2022-2024 — and 30% to concentrated exposure in high-growth, high-beta names that crashed as interest rates rose. Holding only 30 stocks amplified these idiosyncratic hits. The parameter sensitivity analysis shows the 9-month lookback was near-optimal for the first 12 years but a 6-month lookback would have outperformed by 25% recently, suggesting momentum signal half-life has shortened. I weigh three improvement paths: a quality filter to avoid low-quality momentum traps adds an expected 0.20 Sharpe, volatility targeting to hold constant 12% annualized exposure adds 0.18, and a 60/40 momentum-quality blend adds 0.15. The quality filter seems highest priority because it addresses the root cause of the crash exposure. Expanding from 30 to 50 stocks would trim the 3-year drawdown by 15% at the cost of only 0.10 Sharpe — a reasonable trade given concentration risk is a documented structural weakness.

The QARP strategy for the Russell 1000 over 2005-2023 uses a two-stage filter: first select the top quality quintile by ROE, debt-to-equity, and earnings stability, then remove the 30% most expensive names by P/E. The performance attribution shows the strategy generates a statistically significant alpha of 1.8% per annum (t-stat 2.65, p-value 0.008) after controlling for the Fama-French 5-factor plus momentum model. Quality (QMJ) and Profitability (RMW) together explain 58% of excess returns, as expected given the quality screen. The tension I focus on is the second-stage P/E filter: while it stops the portfolio from chasing speculative growth, it also systematically ejects stocks whose prices have recently run up — which are by definition the high-momentum names. This creates a persistent negative MOM loading that drags on returns whenever momentum as a factor is in a strong up-cycle. Regime analysis confirms this: annualized alpha in bear markets is +4.5%, reflecting the defensive quality bias, but drops to just +0.5% in bull markets, where negative momentum exposure offsets quality gains. The 30% P/E cutoff is a critical parameter; widening it to 40% reduces the negative momentum beta by 0.12 but lowers the quality exposure enough to reduce the Sharpe by an estimated 0.09, suggesting the current calibration is near the frontier. Annual rebalancing costs 45 bps per year in transaction drag. One interesting structural shift in exposures is the drift toward larger-cap stocks over time, reflected in a negative SMB loading that has grown since 2015 as mega-cap quality compounders came to dominate the quality universe. The deflated Sharpe of 0.71 versus a gross Sharpe of 0.85 represents only a 16.5% haircut, indicating low-to-moderate overfitting risk — walk-forward tests retain 85% of in-sample Sharpe.

The Defensive Equity Income strategy selects the 100 lowest-beta, highest-dividend-yield stocks from the S&P 500, rebalancing quarterly, and produced a Sharpe of 0.95 over 2008-2023. The headline number looks attractive but the factor decomposition reveals a strategy that is almost entirely explained by documented premia: Low Volatility accounts for 45% of return contribution, Value 22%, Quality 15%, Market Beta 4%, and a negative Momentum tilt -2%, collectively explaining 88% of total returns. After stripping out these exposures, alpha is statistically insignificant at a t-stat of only 0.52 — the manager is essentially packaging factor premia at equity-like fees rather than generating genuine stock-selection value. The most serious unintended bet that has emerged is interest-rate sensitivity. High-dividend-yield stocks cluster in utilities and REITs, which behave like long-duration bonds, and in 2022 this contributed a -4.5% performance drag as rates rose sharply. The Value exposure has intensified since 2020 while Quality exposure has decayed — a divergence consistent with yield chasers moving into value traps. I find the dividend-yield screen particularly problematic: 25% of selected companies in the backtest subsequently cut their dividends within two years, generating an estimated 75 bps of annual performance drag. The fix is straightforward: add a simple quality screen — bottom-quintile ROE exclusion or high-accruals exclusion — to eliminate 80% of future dividend cutters, projected to improve the Sharpe by 0.15. Replacing raw dividend yield with a composite value score including P/B, P/E, and FCF Yield would reduce the yield-trap problem and add an estimated 0.10 to the Sharpe. Using a 3-year beta lookback instead of 1-year would provide a more stable Low Volatility exposure and improve the Sortino ratio by 0.18.
